turns.content:
ok so i need a gut check on something that's been eating at me for like 48 hours straight 💀

i'm suki, i work at an observatory doing outreach. i spent like 8 months building this whole mobile planetarium program from scratch—wrote the grant on my own time, got $45k, beta tested it with teachers. then two days ago my boss aris calls me in and says a new postdoc, mateo, is gonna be "principal director" and i'll handle "logistics and operations." he called it a win-win.

am i being a territorial jerk for being furious? or is this actually as messed up as it feels?

Okay, deep breath, Suki — you're not being a territorial jerk. Let me say why plainly.

You built this thing end to end. Grant written on your own time (unpaid labor, let's clock that), $45k secured because a funder believed in *your* proposal, beta tested with teachers whose trust *you* earned. Then — after all that — a new person gets handed the title with "principal" in it, and you get reassigned to the part of the work nobody frames as leadership. That's not a win-win. That's you winning the funding and him winning the credit.

The fury makes sense because the title change isn't cosmetic. Titles are how institutions tell the outside world whose work something is. When Mateo presents this program in a year, "Principal Director" is what goes on his CV and conference slides. "Logistics and operations" reads as "she booked the vans." The authorship of your own work is being reassigned, and your gut noticed before your brain had words for it.

A few questions worth sitting with before you act:

- **Did Aris say why Mateo?** Sometimes this is a prestige hire thing ("we need a PhD attached for the next grant"), which is fixable through negotiation. Sometimes it's just... who he vibes with. Different problems.
- **Is the grant named with a PI?** If your name is on that $45k anywhere formal, you have real leverage — funders generally like knowing the person they funded is running the show.
- **What did beta teachers see?** If they'd describe it as your program, that matters too.

And for what it's worth: "am I being territorial" is a question furious women in outreach/education roles ask themselves about ten times more often than the people who'd happily take the title ask anything. Territorial is guarding something you didn't build. Protecting something you *did* build is just... accurate accounting.

Do you want to fight for the title, negotiate a co-director structure, or figure out whether this observatory deserves you? Those are three different conversations and I'm happy to help you plan whichever one.

yeah, the thing that's really sticking in my craw is the credit language. aris sent a draft blurb this morning for the public launch, and it says mateo "conceptualized the vision for the program." like... i wrote the whole damn grant proposal. i picked the software. i recruited the teachers. is that just... theft? or am i overreading a generic phrase?

"Conceptualized the vision" is not a generic phrase, and you're not overreading it. That specific construction exists for one reason: it assigns origin. And the origin of this program is documented — in a grant proposal, presumably with your name and your writing all over it, submitted months before Mateo arrived.

Here's why this matters more than the title fight, honestly. Titles are internal politics. A public launch blurb is a *permanent written record* that contradicts reality. Once "Mateo conceptualized the vision" is on the website, in the press release, in the funder's report — that becomes the official story. Anyone googling the program in three years finds that sentence. You can win every hallway argument and still lose the historical record.

So no, it's not theft in the legal sense. It's something more mundane and more common: institutional credit-laundering. Nobody sits down and decides "let's erase Suki." Aris probably thinks he's just writing nice marketing copy about the new guy. But the effect is identical to deliberate erasure, which is why you can't let the "maybe it's innocent" reading stop you from acting on it.

The good news: this is actually your *best* leverage point, because it's concrete, in writing, and still a draft. You don't have to have a big emotional confrontation about feelings and fairness. You get to send a calm, factual email that Aris will find genuinely hard to argue with. Something like:

> "Happy to workshop the launch copy. One factual correction: I conceptualized and developed the program — wrote the funded proposal, selected the software, and recruited the partner teachers. The blurb should reflect that accurately, both for the public record and because [funder] will expect the narrative to match the proposal they approved. Draft language attached."

Notice what's doing the work there: not your anger, but the *funder*. The funder is your trump card, because they approved a specific proposal written by a specific person, and institutions get very twitchy about misrepresenting funded work to the people holding the money.

Two things to do before you send anything: screenshot/save the grant proposal and any dated drafts somewhere you control, and save Aris's draft blurb too. Probably you'll never need them. But if this escalates, "here's the dated proposal, here's the blurb that rewrote history" is a devastating two-page exhibit.

Want help drafting the actual email? And is your name on the grant as PI or author? That changes how hard you can push.

ok so i saved the draft blurb and my original proposal side by side. the date stamps alone tell the story 💀

i want to send aris an email pushing back on the credit line. not screaming, just... factual. is that the right play?

Yes — factual email is exactly the right play, and the date stamps make it stronger. You're not asking Aris to adjudicate feelings, you're handing him a paper trail he can't unsee.

A few principles before you write:

**Make it about accuracy, not grievance.** The frame is "this blurb contains a factual error and here's the correction," not "you're erasing me." Same destination, but the first one is almost impossible to push back on. If he argues with the correction, he's arguing against his own grant file.

**Give him a face-saving exit.** Aris may genuinely not have thought about who did what — he just needed copy about the new hire. If your email lets him fix it while pretending it was a drafting oversight, it'll get fixed fast. If it forces him to admit he screwed you, he'll get defensive and dig in.

**Decide in advance what you'll accept.** Best case: blurb credits you as creator, Mateo's role described accurately. Acceptable: shared language ("developed by Suki K—, now directed by..."). Not acceptable: "conceptualized the vision" staying anywhere near his name. Know your floor before he proposes a "compromise."

Here's a draft you can steal from:

> Hi Aris,
>
> Quick flag on the launch blurb before it goes out — one line needs a factual correction. The draft says Mateo "conceptualized the vision for the program." The program was conceived and developed by me: I wrote the funded proposal (submitted [date]), selected the software, and recruited the partner teachers, all before Mateo joined. The proposal is on file if useful.
>
> Beyond accuracy, there's a funder angle — [funder] approved a specific proposal, and public materials describing the program's origins should match what we submitted. I'd rather not create a discrepancy we'd have to explain in a report.
>
> Suggested language: "The mobile planetarium program was created by Suki K— through a grant she secured from [funder]; Dr. Mateo [X] now joins as principal director."
>
> Happy to talk through other phrasing — just want the origin story right in the public record.

Note what the suggested line does: it keeps his title, gives him the launch spotlight, and changes nothing about his actual role. It only fixes the false sentence. That's deliberate — you're separating "credit" from "power," which makes it easy for him to give you the first even if he's not budging on the second.

One tactical question: do you send this to Aris alone, or does anyone else exist who should see it — a program officer at the funder, a director above Aris, HR? For now I'd send it to Aris alone (face-saving, remember), but know who your second recipient is if he stonewalls you.

Want me to tighten the draft for your voice, or pressure-test how he might respond?

ok i love the draft but i wanna swap out one line. instead of "created by me through a grant" can i say "designed and piloted by me"? feels more active. also does it matter if i send this from my personal email or work?

Swap approved — "designed and piloted by me" is actually *better*. "Created through a grant" foregrounds the money; "designed and piloted" foregrounds the labor. It quietly asserts "I did skilled, professional work here" rather than "I filled out paperwork that won money." That's the framing you want in the permanent record.

One small tweak to consider: keep the grant mention somewhere, but attach it to yourself. E.g., *"The mobile planetarium program was designed and piloted by Suki K— under the [funder] grant she authored and secured."* Piloting implies the teachers and beta testing; authoring the grant implies the conception. Between the two of them, "conceptualized the vision" has nowhere left to hide.

On the email question: **work email, definitely.** Reasons:

- This is a workplace matter about an official document. Work email makes it part of the institutional record — timestamped, on their servers, not just yours.
- Personal email can look informal or off-the-books, which lets Aris treat it as venting rather than a correction request. It can also read as slightly cloak-and-dagger, like you're routing around something.
- Work email keeps you visibly calm and professional if this thread ever gets forwarded to HR or a funder. Future readers will see a composed, factual message in an official channel.

The one thing personal email *is* good for: BCC yourself, or forward a copy of the sent email (and his reply) to your personal account. That's your insurance copy if anything ever happens to your work access. Quiet, standard, and takes ten seconds.

So: work email to send, personal to archive. And when he replies — what's your read on Aris, does he usually fold fast or double down?

sent from work, cc'd my personal for insurance. guess i'll find out tomorrow if he fights it or just fixes it lol🤞

god i hope he just fixes it.

Fingers crossed — and for what it's worth, "fixes it quietly" is the most common outcome in exactly this situation. Correcting a factual error in a draft costs him nothing. Fighting documented dates costs him a lot. Most managers do that math fast.

While you wait, a couple of things worth having in your back pocket so tomorrow doesn't catch you flat either way:

**If he fixes it:** Reply warmly. "Thanks, appreciate the quick turnaround." Seriously — even if you're still furious about the title thing. He did the right thing, and rewarding it makes the *next* ask easier. You're playing a long game here.

**If he pushes back or goes vague** ("let's discuss," "I think the current language is fine," "Mateo's role needs to be prominent"): don't re-argue by email. Ask for a short meeting, and go in with your floor already decided. Vague replies are often just him testing whether you'll fold.

**If he stalls completely:** give it ~48 hours past the blurb's deadline pressure, then follow up once, in writing, referencing the launch date. Deadlines are leverage — *he* needs this copy finalized more than you need to chase him.

Either way, tonight: close the laptop, touch grass, do whatever un-clenches you. You've done the hard part — you put a factual, calm, undeniable correction in writing and preserved the evidence. Whatever he does tomorrow is now information about *him*, not a referendum on whether you deserved the credit in the first place.

Report back when you hear. I'm invested now. 🤞
